title: Project Overview
description: Start with the README to understand the local-first AI workspace, its privacy boundaries, and its supported chat workflows. It frames the two application tracks—an existing Streamlit workspace and the FastAPI plus React v2 architecture—that the rest of the tour connects.

title: Streamlit Workspace
description: The Streamlit entry point is the broadest view of the original interactive workspace: it coordinates conversations, model selection, live generation, presets, and health status. Following it first makes the direct dependencies in the next steps concrete before comparing them with the newer API-driven interface.

title: Models and Runtime
description: These direct dependencies supply the workspace's foundational runtime behavior: local paths, a unified local-or-cloud model catalog, and Ollama discovery and streaming. Together they show the local-first boundary: the UI can select a model while the client encapsulates the actual inference API calls.

title: Documents and Personalization
description: Building on the runtime setup, document ingestion turns uploads into retrieval-ready chunks while personalization derives a compact user profile from conversations and feedback. These features explain how the workspace augments a prompt with locally managed context rather than treating each chat as isolated.

title: FastAPI Application
description: The FastAPI application composes the v2 HTTP surface for conversations, credentials, providers, OAuth, and streaming runs. It is the bridge between the browser-facing React workspace and the same local AI capabilities introduced through the Streamlit flow.

title: API Contracts
description: The backend contracts define the request, response, provider, and run shapes that make the API surface predictable. Reading them after the application entry point clarifies what each endpoint promises before following the provider implementation behind those promises.
languageLesson: Pydantic models turn Python type annotations into validated API schemas, so the same contract describes accepted input and serialized output.

title: Provider Streaming
description: The provider module supplies a common streaming-adapter interface and a registry for Ollama plus optional hosted providers. This design lets the API layer select a provider without embedding provider-specific streaming logic in every endpoint.

title: Local Data and Recall
description: Conversation state, feedback, presets, and exports persist through the SQLite store, while ChromaDB holds vectors for documents, chat history, and memories. These two stores complete the local context story begun in Step 4: durable records and semantic recall serve different roles.

title: React Studio Shell
description: The React bootstrap loads the application under strict mode and an error boundary, and the App component provides navigation, chat, provider management, and workspace pages. This is the client counterpart to the FastAPI composition from Step 5, presenting the API-backed studio in the browser.
languageLesson: React's StrictMode adds development checks around a component tree, while an error boundary keeps a rendering failure from taking down the entire application shell.

title: Build Configuration
description: The Python and frontend manifests define the dependencies, build tooling, tests, and executable entry points for the two tracks. They are the practical map for setting up a development environment that can run both the Streamlit/Python workflow and the Vite/TypeScript workspace.
languageLesson: JSON package manifests make scripts and dependency ranges explicit for JavaScript tooling, while pyproject.toml consolidates Python packaging and tool configuration in a standard TOML file.

title: Learning and Delivery
description: The code tutorial provides module-level architecture and message-flow guidance that reinforces the paths covered in this tour. The CI workflow then turns those expectations into delivery checks by linting and testing the Python backend and installing, linting, testing, and building the React frontend.
languageLesson: GitHub Actions YAML separates event triggers, parallel jobs, and sequential steps, allowing the Python and frontend validation tracks to run consistently on pushes and pull requests.
